# A square can sing the same note in two shapes

[Twenty-five shapes come from one operator. Repeated frequencies tell us something about the square.]{.lesson-deck}
:::

The [beam lesson](../clamped-beam/index.qmd) fixed both displacement and
slope at each end. Program 39 of @trefethen2000 asks the corresponding
question on the square $(-1,1)^2$:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\Delta^2 u=\lambda u, \\
u=\partial_n u=0\quad\text{on all four edges}.
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-plate}

For a uniform thin plate, the dimensional material and length factors
multiply every frequency in the same way. The dimensionless ratios
$\omega_j/\omega_1=\sqrt{\lambda_j/\lambda_1}$ therefore describe the
relative notes without choosing a particular material.

## Assemble a two-dimensional action from one-dimensional operators

The identity $\Delta^2=\partial_x^4+2\partial_x^2\partial_y^2+\partial_y^4$
gives the book's discrete operator

$$
L=I\otimes D_4+D_4\otimes I+2D_2\otimes D_2.
$$ {#eq-tensor}

Here $D_4$ is the weighted clamped operator from the beam chapter, built
from native OpenPFC Chebyshev differentiation. $D_2$ is the ordinary
second-derivative matrix restricted to interior values with zero endpoint
values, as in the book. The complete matrices are formed before restricting
their rows and columns. Simply squaring the interior $D_2$ would impose
a different fourth-order boundary problem.

Keep $x$ as the fastest index. Apply each factor along its own axis:

```{.cpp include="../plate.hpp" snippet="tensor" dedent=2}
```

This action avoids storing a full tensor matrix. The small matrices used
for the eigenproblem below are projections of this same action.

## Let symmetry separate the repeated modes

Reflection in either coordinate leaves the plate unchanged. Choose a
basis whose vectors are even or odd under each reflection. Within the
even/even and odd/odd sectors, also split into shapes that are symmetric
or antisymmetric under $x\leftrightarrow y$.

For an orthonormal nodal basis $Q$, form $Q^T LQ$:

```{.cpp include="../plate.hpp" snippet="symmetry" dedent=4}
```

The example-owned shifted-QR reference solves each small dense block.
It is the same numerical eigenproblem as the book's full matrix; the
symmetry split chooses interpretable shapes inside repeated eigenspaces.
An even/odd mode has an odd/even partner obtained by transposing its
nodal array. Those partners have the same eigenvalue and independent
shapes. Other linear combinations of a repeated pair are equally valid.

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="plate" dedent=4}
```

## Draw a shape that respects the clamp

The display uses a tensor product of the beam's weighted cardinal basis.
Each one-dimensional basis function vanishes with its first derivative
at both endpoints. Values and normal slopes consequently vanish along
every edge of the reconstructed surface:

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="reconstruction" dedent=12}
```

This display uses the constrained polynomial rather than the book's
cubic image interpolation. The mixed derivative in the collocation
operator still uses the book's ordinary $D_2$; it is not redefined by
the display interpolation.

![The first 25 clamped-plate modes at degree 17. Blue and red distinguish the two signs of each normalized shape; black curves mark zero displacement. Each panel gives the mode number and its frequency relative to the fundamental. The sign and orientation of a mode are arbitrary.](figures/plate.svg){#fig-plate .lightbox}

[Open the full-size mode gallery](figures/plate.svg) to inspect individual
nodal lines on a small screen.

## Check the operator, the edges and the eigenspace

The model records all 25 eigenvalues, relative frequencies, symmetry
labels and complete nodal and display fields. It checks the full
operator residual after lifting each reduced eigenvector. The numerical
regression differentiates Lagrange products independently, checks those
residuals, verifies the clamped edges and checks that equal-frequency
partners are independent.

```sh
openpfc run model.cpp input.json --source-root .. --launcher=none
```

Try degree 10 and then 17. Compare the low frequencies before inspecting
the more demanding high modes. Against degree 20, the fundamental
eigenvalue changes by about $6\times10^{-7}$ at degree 10, but the largest
relative change among the first 25 eigenvalues is about $0.29$. At degree
17 those differences fall to about $1.5\times10^{-9}$ and $5.3\times10^{-6}$.
These are comparisons between resolutions, rather than errors against an
exact continuum spectrum. Refinement tests convergence of the
collocation approximation; a small matrix residual alone does not show
that a continuum mode is resolved. This complete-domain teaching
reference runs on one process and accepts degrees 6 through 20.

Keep the [source](model.cpp), [input](input.json), [plate helper](../plate.hpp),
[clamped helper](../clamped.hpp), [eigensolver](../eigensystem.hpp) and
[collocation helper](../collocation.hpp) together.
